parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man enquires about renting a room in a shared house.
script: Hi, I'm calling about the room advertised on the student housing website. Is it still available?
Yes, it is. I'm Margaret, I own the house. What would you like to know?
First, how much is the rent?
It's 520 pounds a month. That includes water and the internet, but electricity and gas are shared between the tenants. Usually that comes to about 40 pounds each a month.
OK. And how many people live there?
There are four bedrooms. At the moment there are three tenants: two nurses who work at the hospital, and a postgraduate student.
Yes. It has a double bed, a wardrobe and a desk. The only thing it doesn't have is a bookshelf, but you could easily add one.
The kitchen is shared, and so is the bathroom. There's also a small garden at the back, which everyone can use.
Is there anywhere to keep a bicycle?
Yes, there's a shed in the garden. It locks, so it's quite safe.
Great. How long is the contract?
The minimum is six months. And I ask for a deposit of one month's rent, which is protected in a government scheme.
The room's free from the 1st of March.
Could I come and see it?
Of course. How about Wednesday evening, at about half past six?
It's 9 Rowan Close. R-O-W-A-N. It's about ten minutes' walk from the university, near the big park.
Thanks. My name's Kenji Watanabe, by the way.
Lovely. See you on Wednesday, Kenji.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A radio presenter gives information about a city's new bike-share scheme.
script: And now some local news. From next Monday, the city's new bike-share scheme, CityCycle, opens to the public, with five hundred bikes at sixty docking stations across the city centre.

To use the scheme, you first need to download the CityCycle app and register a payment card. Unlike the old scheme, there's no need to visit an office to collect a membership card. You unlock a bike by scanning the code on the handlebars with your phone.

There are two ways to pay. Occasional users can pay one pound to unlock a bike and then ten pence a minute. Regular users will probably prefer the monthly pass, which costs 15 pounds and includes unlimited rides of up to forty-five minutes each.
About a third of the bikes are electric. These are more popular with commuters who live on the hills to the north of the city. Electric bikes cost a little more: an extra five pence a minute.
Bikes must be returned to a docking station. If you leave a bike anywhere else, you'll be charged a fine of 20 pounds. The app shows which stations have free spaces, which is useful at busy times.

The council says that, during the trial last summer, the most common complaint was not about the bikes themselves, but about the lack of stations in the suburbs. Twenty new stations will be added outside the centre by the end of the year.

Now, here's where some of the main docking stations are. If you're arriving by train, there's a large station directly outside the main entrance of Central Station. Another is on the corner of King Street and Market Square, opposite the town hall. For students, there's a station inside the university campus, next to the library. Shoppers will find one in the car park of the Riverside Shopping Centre, on the ground floor. And there's also a station by the entrance to Victoria Park, near the lake.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A tutor and two students, Aisha and Felix, discuss a presentation on social media and local businesses.
script: Right, Aisha, Felix. Your presentation is on how small local businesses use social media. Where are you up to?
We've interviewed owners of six businesses: two cafés, a bakery, a bike shop, a hairdresser and a bookshop.
Good mix. What did you find?
The biggest surprise was how little time they spend on it. Most owners said less than an hour a week. They know it's important, but they're too busy running the business.
And most of them said photos of products work far better than special offers. The bakery's most popular post ever was just a picture of bread coming out of the oven.
Interesting. Did any of them pay for advertising?
Only the bike shop. The others said it was too expensive and they couldn't see whether it worked.
And how will you organise the presentation?
We thought we'd start with a short video of one of the café owners talking about her experience. It should grab the audience's attention.
Good idea, but keep it under two minutes. Then what?
Then the main findings, and finally our recommendations for small businesses.
What will your main recommendation be?
To post regularly, even if it's only twice a week, rather than posting a lot and then nothing for weeks. Consistency seemed to matter more than quantity.
That's well supported by the research. One concern: your slides have too much text. The audience will read rather than listen.
We'll cut that down and use more images.
I'll introduce the video and the background. Felix will present the findings, because he did most of the analysis.
And we'll share the recommendations and answer questions together.
Fine. Also, please give each business owner a copy of your findings afterwards. That's good practice when people give you their time.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture about the history of tea.
script: Today's lecture is about tea, which after water is the most widely consumed drink in the world.

Tea comes from a single plant, Camellia sinensis, which is native to the region where China, India and Myanmar meet. Green, black and oolong tea all come from the same leaves; the difference lies in how long the leaves are left to oxidise after they are picked.

For centuries, tea in China was not drunk for pleasure but used as a medicine. It was only during the Tang dynasty, from the seventh century, that tea drinking became a popular custom, and the first book about tea was written at that time.
Tea reached Japan with Buddhist monks, who used it to stay awake during long periods of meditation. Over time this developed into the tea ceremony, in which every movement follows strict rules.

Europeans did not encounter tea until the sixteenth century, through Portuguese and Dutch traders. In Britain, tea was at first so expensive that it was kept in locked boxes, and only the wealthy could afford it. Heavy taxes led to widespread smuggling; at one point, more tea entered Britain illegally than legally. When the tax was cut sharply in 1784, tea became affordable for ordinary people almost overnight.

The British also wanted to end their dependence on China. In the nineteenth century they began growing tea in India, first in Assam, where a local variety of the plant was discovered, and later in Darjeeling. Workers on these plantations often faced very harsh conditions.

Finally, a modern invention: the tea bag. It was discovered by accident in the early twentieth century, when an American merchant sent samples of tea in small silk bags. Customers assumed the bags were meant to be put directly into the pot. Today, in Britain, around ninety-six per cent of tea is made with tea bags.

passages.title: Summer activities for children at Millbrook Library
paras: A  Story Explorers (ages 3-5). Stories, songs and crafts every Tuesday morning. Parents must stay with their children. Free, no booking needed.
B  Code Club (ages 9-13). Learn to build simple games on the library computers. Thursdays, 2-4 pm, six weeks. Free, but places must be booked, as there are only twelve computers.
C  Summer Reading Challenge (ages 4-11). Read six library books over the summer and collect stickers and a medal. Sign up at any time at the children's desk.

D  Young Writers' Workshop (ages 12-16). Three sessions with a published author to write and edit your own short story. £15 for all three sessions. The best story will be printed in the local newspaper.
E  Lego Builders (ages 6-10). Build models on a different theme each week. Saturday mornings. Children over 8 may attend without an adult.

passages.title: Northway Bank: dress code for staff
paras: Staff who work with customers in branches must wear the company uniform, which is provided free of charge. Two shirts or blouses and one jacket are supplied each year; extra items can be bought at cost price.
Staff in head office do not wear uniform but should dress in a business-casual style. Jeans may be worn on Fridays, provided they are clean and not torn.
Trainers are not permitted in branches, but are acceptable in head office if they are plain and in good condition.
Name badges must be worn by all branch staff. Badges may show a first name only, if the employee prefers.
Staff may wear religious or cultural dress. Managers should be contacted if any adjustment to the uniform is needed, for example a uniform-coloured headscarf, which the company will provide.
Visible tattoos are allowed, except where they contain offensive words or images.

passages.title: Applying for a work permit for a seasonal job: frequently asked questions
paras: A  Who needs a permit? Anyone who is not a citizen of this country and wishes to work here for up to six months in farming, tourism or hospitality. You cannot apply if you already hold another type of work permit.
B  When should I apply? Applications open three months before the season starts. Processing usually takes four to six weeks, so apply early.
C  What documents do I need? A valid passport, a written job offer from a registered employer, and proof that you have enough money to support yourself for the first month.
D  How much does it cost? The fee is 120 euros. It is not refunded if your application is refused.
E  Can I change employer? Yes, but only within the same industry, and you must inform the immigration office within ten days.
F  Can my family come with me? No. Seasonal permits are for the worker only. Family members must apply separately for a visitor visa.

passages.title: Why we procrastinate
paras: A  Almost everyone puts things off sometimes, but for an estimated one in five adults, procrastination is a chronic problem that affects their work, finances and health. For many years it was treated as a matter of poor time management: people simply needed better plans and calendars. More recent research suggests that this view misses the point.

B  According to psychologist Tim Pychyl, procrastination is not a time-management problem but an emotion-management problem. People delay tasks that make them feel anxious, bored or insecure. Putting the task off brings immediate relief, which makes the behaviour more likely to happen again. The cost, unfortunately, is paid later, often with interest.

C  Brain-imaging studies support this idea. They suggest that chronic procrastinators may have a larger amygdala, the part of the brain associated with processing threats, and weaker connections between this area and the regions involved in planning. In other words, the immediate discomfort of a task can outweigh the knowledge that it needs to be done.

D  Procrastination also involves the way we think about our future selves. When researchers asked people to think about themselves in ten years' time, brain activity looked similar to when they thought about a stranger. If our future self feels like someone else, it is easier to leave our problems for them to deal with. Interestingly, people who were shown digitally aged images of their own faces later saved more money for retirement.

E  What helps? Strict schedules and willpower alone tend to fail. Pychyl recommends making the first step as small as possible, for example 'open the document' rather than 'write the report'. Once a task has started, it is usually less unpleasant than expected. Another approach is self-compassion. A study of university students found that those who forgave themselves for procrastinating on one exam were less likely to procrastinate before the next one. Criticising yourself, it seems, simply adds to the negative feelings that caused the delay.

F  Not all delay is harmful. Some researchers distinguish 'active procrastination', in which people deliberately postpone a task because they work well under pressure, and still finish on time. Whether this really produces better work, or simply feels that way, remains a matter of debate.
